lesson.title: Loyalty or Silence: Wartime Laws That Tested the Bill of Rights
lesson.summary: Congress passed the Espionage Act in 1917 and the far harsher Sedition Act in 1918 to punish opposition to the war, laws that led to the imprisonment of prominent dissenters like socialist leader Eugene Debs and raised serious, lasting concerns about free speech under the Bill of Rights.
lesson.body:
The intense wartime nationalism cultivated by the Committee on Public Information, discussed in the previous chapter, did not stop at persuasion. The federal government also moved to criminalize dissent outright, worried that antiwar speech might undermine the draft described earlier or weaken support for the war more broadly. The result was two of the most restrictive laws on political speech in American history.

The Espionage Act, passed on June 15, 1917, made it a crime to obtain information that could damage U.S. military operations or assist an enemy. Critically, it also criminalized willfully causing or attempting to cause insubordination within the armed forces and willfully obstructing military recruitment or enlistment, provisions that reached well beyond traditional spying and into ordinary political speech. In May 1918, Congress went further still, passing the Sedition Act as an amendment to the Espionage Act. This law criminalized using, in its own words, disloyal, profane, scurrilous, or abusive language about the United States government, the Constitution, the flag, or the military uniform, effectively outlawing broad categories of criticism of the war and of the government itself.

Enforcement of these laws led to more than a thousand prosecutions across the country. The most famous case involved Eugene V. Debs, the longtime Socialist Party leader and repeat presidential candidate, who was sentenced in 1918 to ten years in prison for a speech he gave in Canton, Ohio, criticizing the draft and the war. Debs ran for president again in 1920, campaigning from behind prison walls, and still won roughly 900,000 votes. Socialist and labor newspapers lost their mailing privileges at the discretion of the Postmaster General, and many ordinary citizens faced investigation or arrest simply for private conversations critical of the war effort. In the 1919 case Schenck v. United States, the Supreme Court unanimously upheld an Espionage Act conviction against Charles Schenck, a Socialist Party official who had distributed leaflets urging resistance to the draft. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes, writing for the Court, introduced the now-famous clear and present danger test and compared Schenck's leaflets to falsely shouting fire in a crowded theater.

It is important to be honest about what these laws actually did. Historians and civil liberties advocates have long viewed the Espionage and Sedition Acts, and especially their aggressive enforcement, as a serious overreach that punished legitimate political dissent and criticism of government policy far more often than it caught any genuine espionage or sabotage. The laws chilled free speech and a free press at a scale rarely seen before or since in American history, a sobering example of how wartime fear can erode the very constitutional protections, including freedom of speech guaranteed under the Bill of Rights, that the country claimed to be fighting for. Reflecting a shift in attitude once the war had ended, the Sedition Act was repealed in 1920, and many of the harshest sentences handed down under it, including Debs's, were later commuted.
